claims.text: Coupling enhanced free-energy sampling with machine-learning interatomic potentials will enable efficient determination of melting and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
The target materials are HEA solid solutions spanning broad multi-principal-element compositional space.
The proposed framework couples metadynamics or umbrella sampling with ML-trained interatomic potentials.
The framework is intended to operate across the solid-to-liquid transition and within the high-temperature liquid phase.
The framework is applicable to compositions representative of the full compositional diversity of the HEA family.
The computed free-energy landscape will capture transient atomic rearrangements and nucleation events during melting.
ML interatomic potentials can provide accurate atomic interactions for HEA simulations.
Enhanced free-energy sampling efficiently overcomes intrinsic free-energy barriers associated with rapid phase transitions.
ML-optimized interatomic potentials provide high energetic fidelity.
ML-optimized interatomic potentials provide substantial computational speed.
The combined approach accurately maps HEA melting processes and liquid-state properties.
The framework will predict melting temperature, enthalpy and entropy of fusion, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties.
Predicted thermodynamic properties will have errors of roughly 5% or less relative to high-precision experiments.
The proposed framework will be much more efficient than traditional calorimetry or CALPHAD-based methods.
Differential scanning calorimetry and CALPHAD are typically too time-consuming or insufficiently accurate across broad HEA composition space.
Insufficient ML training data for extremely high-melting or refractory alloys may increase computational effort or cause errors exceeding 5%.
Existing evidence shows that accurate interatomic-potential simulations can capture finite-temperature properties and atomic-scale mechanisms in selected HEAs.
Deviation greater than approximately 5% for any key property in at least three distinct HEA compositions would falsify the proposed approach.
